summary: Hamilton County lookout from 1909, with a 47-foot steel tower from 1920; removed in the 1980s, and its parts rebuilt as an exhibit at the Adirondack History Museum in Elizabethtown.

facts.status_note: The original tower came down. A tower rebuilt from its parts stands inside the Adirondack History Museum in Elizabethtown.

access.note: The rebuilt tower is inside the Adirondack History Museum in Elizabethtown; visitors enter the museum to climb it. No source we read describes the original mountain site today.

visit.trail_note: Climbing is inside the museum, not at the mountain site.

events.note: Lookout established on a 12-foot tower at a cost of $1,064.44 (Forest Lookouts)

Conservation Commission replaced the original tower with a 47-foot Aermotor LS-40 steel tower
New cabin for the observer's living quarters constructed (Forest Lookouts)
Fire lookout operations ceased at the end of the 1970 season because of aerial detection

corrections.why: The stored value is a fragment of the 1909 source line, not an agency name. The steel tower of 1920 was built by the Conservation Commission.
3.7 m (12 ft) describes the 1909 tower. The 47-foot steel tower built in 1920 is 14.3 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register calls the Elizabethtown host the Adirondack History Museum; Starr and Wikipedia name the Essex County Historical Society or Museum. Both describe the same building.
The 1909 entry is a 12-foot lookout (Forest Lookouts). The 47-foot steel tower dates from 1920 (Starr, Wikipedia, Forest Lookouts).

sources.title: Fire Towers of New York list, Bill Starr

notes_for_editor: Unresolved: the 1909 12-foot lookout (Forest Lookouts) versus Wikipedia's 1899 14-foot USGS signal tower as the first structure; the pages do not say whether they are the same. Elevation: Starr and the CNY list give 2,913 ft; Wikipedia gives 2,923 ft. Removal date: NHLR says the 1980s; Wikipedia says 'later removed' with no date; Starr gives none. No source we read describes the mountain site today. The Elizabethtown tower is a reassembly of parts, not the original. The access level 'public' for the museum tower is our reading of the NHLR note that visitors enter the museum to climb it; check museum hours before publishing.
